title: Terraform Plan, State, and Failure Decisions

questions.question: A resource block is renamed, but the existing remote object must stay in place. What should the configuration include before planning?
options: A moved block from the old resource address to the new address
A lifecycle ignore_changes rule for every attribute
A second provider block with the old address
The -refresh=false planning option
questions.explanation: A moved block tells Terraform to rebind the existing object from the old configuration address to the new one before constructing the plan. Without it, the rename normally looks like removal plus creation.

questions.question: When should depends_on be preferred over an expression reference?
options: Whenever two resources use the same provider
Whenever the downstream resource has an unknown value
When a hidden behavioral dependency exists but the downstream block consumes no upstream attribute
To make every resource run sequentially
questions.explanation: Expression references communicate both data flow and ordering and are preferred when possible. depends_on is for dependencies Terraform cannot infer from referenced values.

questions.question: What does a normal terraform plan do before comparing configuration with prior state?
options: It applies all non-destructive changes automatically
It reads managed remote objects to refresh Terraform's current view
It writes a saved plan file by default
It disables state locking to avoid delays
questions.explanation: Normal planning refreshes managed objects, then compares configuration, prior state, and refreshed values. The -refresh=false option skips those remote reads and can produce an incomplete plan.

questions.question: Run B begins while Run A is applying against the same state. What is the strongest default containment?
options: Two local state files with the same resource bindings
Running both applies with -lock=false
Using -target in both runs
A backend that supports state locking, with locking enabled and a bounded lock timeout
questions.explanation: State locking serializes writers for a shared state when the backend supports it. Disabling locks allows concurrent operations to act from competing snapshots.

questions.question: A Terraform apply fails after some resources were changed successfully. What happens next?
options: Terraform automatically rolls back every completed remote API operation
Terraform records completed changes it knows about, unlocks state, exits, and requires a fresh reconciliation plan
Terraform deletes the state so the next run starts clean
Terraform applies the remaining nodes without another plan
questions.explanation: Terraform does not provide transactional rollback for a partially completed apply. Operators must resolve the error, inspect state and remote objects, and generate a fresh plan.

questions.question: Why is applying the saved plan reviewed by automation stronger than reviewing a speculative plan and later running terraform apply with no plan file?
options: Saved plans never contain sensitive data
Speculative plans always skip refresh
The saved-plan workflow applies the same planned artifact that policy and humans reviewed
Saved plans make provider APIs transactional
questions.explanation: An unsaved plan is speculative. A later apply without that file generates a new plan. Saved plans can contain sensitive values, so they must be protected even when they strengthen review-to-apply continuity.

questions.question: For the current Terraform S3 backend, which setting enables S3 lockfile-based state locking?
options: parallelism = 1
skip_credentials_validation = true
workspace_key_prefix = "lock"
use_lockfile = true
questions.explanation: The S3 backend documents use_lockfile = true for S3 lockfile-based locking. DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated; this setting is specific to the S3 backend, not a universal backend argument.
